about.title: About
about.p1: Dr. Hao Wang served as a Lecturer in the Department of Intelligence Science and Technology at Shanghai University from 2019 to 2024, and has been an Associate Professor since 2024. Since 2025, he has been seconded to the Putuo District Data Bureau in Shanghai, serving as Deputy Director of the Administrative Approval Center and Deputy Director of the Urban Operations Center. He received a doctoral fellowship from the China Scholarship Council and earned his M.Sc. (2014) and Ph.D. (2019) from Waseda University, Japan. He has worked at Microsoft Research Asia, Toshiba Global R&D, and NTT Communication Science Laboratories. He has published more than 50 papers in international conferences and journals, including ACL, COLING, EMNLP, IJCAI, and CSCW. More than 40 of these papers have appeared in SCI/SSCI/A&HCI-indexed venues or CCF-recommended conferences. He has led a completed Shanghai Municipal Science and Technology Commission Sailing Program project, an NSFC Young Scientists Fund project at the AI interdisciplinary interface, and five industry collaboration projects. As a key member, he has also contributed to several NSFC major and general projects, the National Key R&D Program, and special projects on social governance. His research interests include artificial intelligence, human–AI collaborative cognition, and natural language processing, with applications in medical and other high-stakes documents.

expectations.title: To Prospective Students
paragraphs: Over the past year, I made 4,193 contributions on GitHub.

At H!NT Lab, we care less about titles or polished resumes, and more about whether people are willing to do real work. Research and engineering are not built by talk alone. They take code, debugging, trial and error, and steady progress over time.

We welcome students from different universities and academic disciplines. Undergraduate institution and original major are not our main selection criteria. We place greater value on research interests, independent learning, concrete action, and sustained commitment. You may have a weak foundation, come from a non-CS background, or have little experience at the beginning. What matters is whether you are willing to learn, try things yourself, and take one concrete step forward when facing a real problem.

Your first code may be rough. Your first idea may be naive. That is fine. What I value is whether you have actually tried, whether you can explain what you did, where you got stuck, and how you plan to improve.
If you would like to contact me, please first read one of the projects on this page and briefly answer the following three questions in your email:
Which problem or direction interests you?
What do you think this project is trying to solve?
If you were to get involved, what small step would you try first? This could be a piece of code, a simple experiment, a literature review, or a concrete analysis.
There is no need for a long self-introduction or a generic statement of interest. I would rather see a small sign of real thinking and action.
Your starting point matters less than your willingness to act. I look forward to working with students who are ready to learn by doing and to build something meaningful together.

openQuestions.title: Open questions
openQuestions.summary: We welcome discussion and collaboration on these questions.

items.title: How can multiple agents collaborate reliably?
items.body: When agents work together, how should permissions and evidence be organized so people can correct mistakes and take over?

items.title: How can systems adapt to changing information and rules?
items.body: As documents and knowledge change, how can rules and memory be updated while keeping a record of what changed and why?

items.title: When should AI act, and when should people decide?
items.body: When should a system execute, ask, or wait? How should we assess reliability, cognitive load, and human control?
